Shamefacedness
SHAYM-fayst-nes
n.
From shamefaced (originally shamefast, “held fast by shame”) + -ness. The 1611 KJV translators rendered the Greek aidōs as shamefacedness in 1 Timothy 2:9—the deep, inward sense of modesty that knows what would be shameful and naturally inclines away from it.

📖 Biblical Definition

Shamefacedness, in the King James Bible, renders the Greek aidōs—the deep, inward sense of modesty that has a healthy awareness of what would be shameful and naturally inclines the soul away from it. Paul commands it of Christian women in 1 Timothy 2:9: in like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array. The word is paired with sobriety (the cousin virtue of self-controlled soundness of mind) as the inner disposition that produces modest outward adornment, with the negative counterpart spelled out: not the conspicuous display of hair-art, jewelry, gold, and costly clothing that announces the wearer’s status, wealth, or sexual self-presentation. The deeper biblical category, however, extends beyond apparel. Shamefacedness is the regenerate soul’s inward sensitivity to what is shameful: the modesty that does not want to be exposed in immodest ways, the sensitivity that knows what ought to remain private, the reverence that does not want to display before God or men what God has called the saint to keep covered. In a fallen world, the loss of shamefacedness is one of the most diagnostic spiritual symptoms: where shame has been removed from what God has called shameful (the public display of nakedness, the exhibition of perversion, the boasting in what ought to be wept over, the parading of intimate matters before a watching audience), the soul has lost an inward register essential to its protection. Conversely, the recovery of shamefacedness is one of the surest marks of regenerate life: the new heart has been given an inward sensitivity to sin that the old heart did not possess, and the believer finds himself wanting to cover what he once would have displayed, to keep private what he once would have boasted, to flee from what he once would have pursued. The Pauline doctrine is therefore that shamefacedness is no relic of repressive culture but the proper interior disposition of a regenerate soul living modestly before God and others in a world that has, by the curse, much to be ashamed of, and much grace by which the redeemed are clothed.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SHAMEFACED as bashful; easily confused or put out of countenance; modest; in scripture, the deep inward modesty that knows what would be shameful and inclines the soul away from it.

expand to see more

SHAMEFACED, a. — Bashful; easily confused or put out of countenance; modest. In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety (1 Tim 2:9).

SHAMEFACEDNESS, n. — Bashfulness; excess of modesty; the inward sense of modesty that becomes a regenerate person, especially in apparel and bearing.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Timothy 2:9-10 — "In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array; But (which becometh women professing godliness) with good works."

1 Peter 3:3-4 — "Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price."

Proverbs 11:22 — "As a jewel of gold in a swine’s snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion."

Romans 1:27 — "And likewise also the men, leaving the natural use of the woman, burned in their lust one toward another; men with men working that which is unseemly..."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Shamefacedness is corrupted, in the present age, by the systematic removal of shame from what God has called shameful (the public exhibition of nakedness, the celebration of perversion, the parading of intimate matters before watching audiences)—and by the inverse corruption in some traditions of attaching shame to ordinary bodily realities God has not called shameful, producing a brittle puritanism rather than the deep Christian modesty Scripture commends.

expand to see more

The systematic removal of shame from what God has called shameful is the most visible and most pastorally damaging contemporary corruption. The public exhibition of nakedness has become unremarkable in entertainment, advertising, and increasingly in daily life; the celebration of perversion has been institutionally normalized; the parading of intimate matters before watching audiences (social media, reality television, the public exhibition of relationships, sexuality, mental life) has trained a generation out of the inward sensitivity Scripture calls shamefacedness. The believer who absorbs the surrounding register loses, often unconsciously, the regenerate disposition that wants to cover what God has called shameful and to keep private what God has called private. Recover the doctrine, and the saint recovers also the inward register: a modesty in apparel, in speech, in the publication of his life, in what he watches and reads and admits to his eye—not as repression of the body or the affections, but as the proper deference of a creature living before the holy God in a world where much is shameful and much grace is given by which the redeemed are clothed.

The opposite corruption is the brittle puritanism that attaches shame to ordinary bodily realities God has not called shameful. The body itself is not shameful; sexuality within marriage is not shameful; the proper enjoyment of God’s creation is not shameful. Where a tradition has attached shame to these, it has produced a distortion of biblical shamefacedness that confuses the saint, oppresses the conscience with imaginary obligations, and often produces the very secret indulgences the over-shaming was meant to prevent. The biblical balance is precise. Shame attaches to what God has called shameful (sin, the public display of nakedness outside its proper marital context, the celebration of perversion, the boasting in what ought to be wept over); shame does not attach to what God has called good (the body itself, marital intimacy, the proper enjoyment of food, drink, beauty, and play within His ordinances). Recover both ends, and shamefacedness recovers its biblical shape: a deep inward modesty that knows what God has called shameful and inclines the soul away from it, paired with a confident enjoyment of what God has called good and a refusal to be shamed by what He has not.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek aidōs (modesty, shamefacedness—1 Tim 2:9; Heb 12:28); cousin Greek aischunē (shame); Hebrew bōsh (to be ashamed) and kelimmāh (shame)—the deep inward sensitivity to what is shameful that inclines the regenerate soul to modesty in apparel, speech, and self-publication.

expand to see more

Greek aidōs (G127) — modesty, shamefacedness, reverence (1 Tim 2:9; Heb 12:28).

Greek aischunē (G152) — shame (the cousin word for the felt experience of being shamed).

Hebrew bōsh (H954) — to be ashamed, put to shame.

Hebrew kelimmāh (H3639) — shame, disgrace.

Usage

"That women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety—the inward disposition producing the outward modesty."

"Shamefacedness is the regenerate soul’s inward sensitivity to what God has called shameful, paired with the confident enjoyment of what He has called good."

"The systematic removal of shame from what God has called shameful is the more visible contemporary corruption; brittle puritanism that attaches shame to what He has not is the inverse."
